newsitem.title: USA: Hillary Clinton says Americans weak on foreign aid.
newsitem.headline: Hillary Clinton says Americans weak on foreign aid.

text.p: First lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Monday said opposition to foreign aid had lessened in the U.S. Congress but the United States had missed good opportunities in Russia and Eastern Europe for lack of more aid.

"We have seen a change in attitude and a greater awareness on the part of the Congress, but I still think there is a case to be made to the general public," she told reporters, noting foreign assistance has long been misunderstood by Americans.

Mrs. Clinton spoke at a White House briefing accompanied by Thomas Pickering, the newly installed undersecretary of state for political affairs, and Brian Atwood, the head of the Agency for International Development.
The first lady joins President Bill Clinton, members of Congress and business leaders on Tuesday to highlight plans to promote economic growth in Africa.
Noting that foreign aid was an early target when Republicans took control of Congress in the 1994 elections, Mrs. Clinton said the situation has improved.
"We have seen attitudes among members of Congress...begin to change as they have tackled problems and traveled," she said.
Asked if Washington was "doing enough" to help Russian President Boris Yeltsin, she replied "probably not."
"I think that we've missed some real opportunities, not just in Russia but in Central and Eastern Europe to make more investments in democratization efforts and development assistance," she said.
"We've cut our direct aid to Russia rather dramatically, and I think that is something that we should rethink," she said.
Mrs. Clinton has used many of her foreign trips to underscore the effectiveness of U.S. foreign aid, frequently visiting projects that have benefitted directly from it.
Mrs. Clinton, who visited six African countries this year, will participate in a White House program on Tuesday to promote increased trade and investments in Africa.

She said there "still is not a very broad or deep understanding out in the public at large" and opinion polls show that Americans feel the U.S. government spends too much on foreign aid, mistakenly believing that as much as 15 to 25 percent of the federal budget goes to aiding other countries.
When most Americans are asked how much should be spent on foreign aid, "often people say...no more than 10 percent, and yet we spend less than one" percent of the budget, she said.
"So there is a real disconnect," she said.

"I think a lot of Americans are proud when they hear that we've wiped out polio in both the North and the South Americas, and many other examples that we could give ... but they still don't have a good factual understanding of what we spend our money on, how much we spend and the results we get."
